([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).

$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability
([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]).

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density
version: this definition does not assert that $f\mapsto f(x)$ is
identifiable from the law $P_f$.

For a Borel normalized kernel $K$, $h>0$ and $n\ge1$, the map
$$Q_h:(\mathbb R^d)^n\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R,\qquad (z_1,\ldots,z_n,x)\mapsto\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-z_i}{h}\right)$$
is Borel measurable for the finite product Borel sigma-algebra.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $f$ be a density version in
$W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d)$, and let $K$ be a normalized Borel kernel with
$K\in L^1$, $\int u_jK(u)\,du=0$ for every $j$, and
$$M_2(K):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}|K(u)|\,\|u\|^2du<\infty.$$
Define the convolution $S_hf=\int K(u)f(\cdot-hu)du$ as an $L^2$ equivalence
class. With
$$\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2:=\sum_{j,k=1}^d\|\partial_{jk}f\|_{L^2}^2,$$
one has, for every $h>0$,
$$\|S_hf-f\|_{L^2}\le\frac{h^2}{2}M_2(K)\,\|D^2f\|_{2,F}.$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

If $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable and $\int f\,d\mu<+\infty$, then
$f(x)<+\infty$ for almost every $x$.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: For fixed $h$, [F2] makes $(z,x)\mapsto\widehat f_h(x)$ Borel, and [F1] makes $f(x)$ Borel as a function of $(z,x)$. Arithmetic measurability in [F2] therefore makes the squared error product-measurable and nonnegative. Tonelli [F6] identifies MISE with the integral over $x$ of its expected pointwise squared error, even before finiteness has been established.

Write $q_h(x,z)=h^{-d}K((x-z)/h)$. By Tonelli and the substitution $z+hu$ in [F8], $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbb E|q_h(x,X_1)|dx=\|K\|_1, \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}\mathbb E[q_h(x,X_1)^2]dx =h^{-d}\|K\|_2^2.$ Consequently, [F9] makes the summands integrable and square-integrable for almost every $x$. Thus both parts have finite density integrals, and [F7] applied separately to them, followed by subtraction using [F11], gives $\mathbb E q_h(x,X_1)=\int g(z)f(z)dz$. Signed substitution [F8] then identifies this integral with $S_hf(x)$, and identical laws plus finite-sum linearity [F11] give $\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)=S_hf(x)$.

At almost every $x$ from step 2.1, the variables $q_h(x,X_i)$ are iid and square-integrable. Set $W_i=q_h(x,X_i)-\mathbb E q_h(x,X_i)$. These are independent, integrable and square-integrable by [F5] and step 2.1; for $i\ne j$, [F5] makes $W_iW_j$ integrable and gives $\mathbb E[W_iW_j]=\mathbb EW_i\,\mathbb EW_j=0$. Expanding the finite square in the variance definition [F10] and applying [F11] gives $\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x))=n^{-2}\sum_i\mathbb EW_i^2=\operatorname{Var}(q_h(x,X_1))/n$. Expanding one centered square using [F10]–[F11] gives $\operatorname{Var}(q_h(x,X_1))=\mathbb E[q_h(x,X_1)^2]-(\mathbb E q_h(x,X_1))^2\le\mathbb E[q_h(x,X_1)^2]$. Integrating and using step 2.1 bounds the integrated variance by $\|K\|_2^2/(nh^d)$.

For almost every $x$, step 2.1 identifies the bias with $S_hf(x)-f(x)$. The $L^2$ bound [F3] therefore gives $\int_{\mathbb R^d}(\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2dx \le\frac{h^4}{4}M_2(K)^2\|D^2f\|_{2,F}^2.$

At almost every $x$, expand $\widehat f_h(x)-f(x)=(\widehat f_h(x)-\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x))+(\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))$. The centered term has expectation zero, so [F10]–[F11] give $\mathbb E[(\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2] =\operatorname{Var}(\widehat f_h(x)) +(\mathbb E\widehat f_h(x)-f(x))^2.$ Integrate this nonnegative identity using step 1.1, then apply steps 3.1 and 3.2 to obtain the displayed MISE bound. Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does

integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything

companion page.

statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Fix an integer $d\ge1$. A **density version** on $\mathbb R^d$ is a Borel
function $f:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ with
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}f\,d\lambda_d=1.$$
Write $P_f=f\,d\lambda_d$ for its probability law
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Let $\Theta$ be any set of such density
versions. For sample size $n\ge1$, the iid experiment has data space
$$\left((\mathbb R^d)^n,\bigotimes_{i=1}^n\mathcal B(\mathbb R^d)\right)$$
and sampling law $P_f^{\otimes n}$ at parameter $f\in\Theta$
([[def-statistical-experiment]], [[def-parametric-statistical-model]],
[[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]],
[[def-independent-random-elements]],
[[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]],
[[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]]).
The pointwise target at $x\in\mathbb R^d$ is the estimand
$$\psi_x(f)=f(x):\Theta\to\mathbb R$$
([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]]).

A **normalized kernel** is a Borel function $K:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ with
$K\in L^1(\lambda_d)$ and $\int K\,d\lambda_d=1$. It may be signed. For
bandwidth $h>0$ and observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the kernel density estimate
is the indexed family
$$\widehat f_h(x)=\frac1{nh^d}\sum_{i=1}^n K\!\left(\frac{x-X_i}{h}\right),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$
For each fixed $x$, this is intended as a real-valued estimator of $\psi_x$;
the next local lemma supplies its measurability

Assuming $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, if $K$ is pointwise nonnegative the estimate
is a probability density for every sample, as proved in
[[lem-nonnegative-kde-integrates-to-one]]. For a signed kernel the estimate
need not be nonnegative. Point evaluation depends on the selected density

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

$$\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,d(x,y)=\pi.$$
